w: Designed by Italian engineer Battista Antonelli to guard Havana's harbor mouth, this fortress was Spain's main defense for over a century -- until the British captured it outright in 1762. Spain got it back a year later under the Treaty of Paris, and it held the job until La Cabaña took over in 1774.

w: Cuban sculptor Jilma Madera won the competition to design this hilltop figure of Christ in 1953, and it has watched over Havana's bay ever since -- a quieter cousin of Rio's Corcovado, carved by a woman in a field then dominated by men, on a hill that offers one of the city's best views back toward the old town.

w: Havana's Galician immigrant community paid for this Belgian-designed theater in 1914, raised on the site of the demolished Teatro Tacón as a community hall as much as a stage. It's been home to the Cuban National Ballet since, and every two years hosts the International Ballet Festival of Havana, running since 1960.

w: At the end of Calle Obispo, this cocktail bar built its reputation on daiquiris and one famous regular: Hemingway drank here so often a life-size bronze of him now leans permanently at his old spot at the bar. A plaque nearby carries his own verdict on Havana's rival bars -- mojito at the Bodeguita, daiquiri here.

w: Since 1942, this bar has claimed to be the birthplace of the Mojito, a claim historians dispute but drinkers rarely question. Salvador Allende and Pablo Neruda both drank here, and the walls are buried under decades of signatures from everyone who came through -- a visitors' book scribbled onto the plaster.

claims to be the birthplace of the Mojito, a disputed claim

w: Opened in 1958 as the glittering Habana Hilton, this 25-floor tower had barely opened before history rewrote its purpose: after revolutionaries took Havana, Castro moved in and ran the country from its rooms through 1959. It has operated as the Habana Libre since, one hotel that briefly doubled as a capital.

w: Raised on Taganana Hill above the Vedado seafront in 1930, this Spanish-eclectic hotel has traded on its view ever since. The terraced grounds and twin towers overlook the Malecón and the sea beyond, a vantage point that made it one of Havana's grandest addresses for the better part of a century.

w: Every Spanish governor of Havana once ruled from this Baroque palace on the Plaza de Armas, later serving as City Hall. n: Our Lady of Kazan Orthodox Cathedral
w: On a corner overlooking Havana Harbour, this gold-domed cathedral answers to the Russian Orthodox Church rather than Rome -- an unexpected outpost of Moscow's faith in the heart of Old Havana, a legacy of the decades-long alliance between Cuba and the Soviet Union that still has a working congregation today.

w: Built between 1748 and 1777 on the Plaza de la Catedral, this baroque cathedral once held stranger cargo than sacraments: Christopher Columbus's remains sat inside from 1796 to 1898, before being shipped off to Seville. Seat of Havana's archdiocese since 1782, its twin asymmetrical towers define the city's skyline.

w: President Gerardo Machado commissioned this domed capitol in 1926, and architect Eugenio Rayneri Piedra had it finished within three years -- a monument to state power raised by a leader whose own grip on it would soon slip. Machado was gone within a decade; El Capitolio has outlasted him by nearly a century.

w: This was the seat of every Cuban president from Mario García Menocal to Fulgencio Batista -- and in 1957, two years before the revolution, students of the Directorio Revolucionario stormed it trying to reach Batista inside his own palace. It became the Museum of the Revolution not long after the revolutionaries won.

w: Officially Avenida de Maceo, this 8-km seawall was built to keep the sea's winter storm swells, the frentes frios, from battering facades along San Lazaro. w: A star-shaped tower rises over the Plaza de la Revolución, guarding a statue of José Martí ringed by six columns and gardens -- holding, by most accounts, the title of largest monument built for a writer. Preserved as a museum, like his house in Key West, it still holds his books, his boat and the rooms he worked in, largely as he left them.

n: Basílica Menor de San Francisco de Asís
w: Construction on this Franciscan basilica began in 1548 and dragged on so long it was inaugurated in 1575 unfinished -- then an 1694 hurricane knocked its tower down, forcing a rebuild from 1716. In 1842, in one of Old Havana's odder swaps, the church became the general post office, a job it held for decades.
